_README: ATC's own Trail Updates, as reviewed by a person, keyed by ATC's slug.
features/ATC_TRAIL_UPDATES.md is the design. export_atc_updates.py bakes
this file into conditions/atc_updates.json, which the app reads as the
ATC's word rather than as OurHike's (#459, #460, #461).
EDITED BY HAND, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN RATHER THAN A STOPGAP. ATC
publishes these as prose on their website, in NOBO miles from Springer -
the same number as `closures.start_mile_marker`. Parsing that is easy and
is already proven (spike_atc_updates.py: seven of nine live updates carry
a placeable mile reference). What is not automatable is deciding whether
a parsed range is RIGHT, and three specific things go wrong:
- A regex produces a confident wrong answer. `NOBO mile 1,503.6` read
without the thousands separator is mile 1: a Connecticut shelter
drawn in Georgia. It parses, it looks plausible, it is 1,502 miles
wrong, and no schema check catches it.
- Some updates END a closure. 'NC/TN: Iron Mtn Gap Reopened' means the
trail is open again. An ingest that only ever adds closures
accumulates barriers across trail people have been walking for weeks.
- One update can state several ranges, accumulated over months of
edits, and the current one is not mechanically distinguishable from
its own history.
So: a person reads ATC's page, writes the rows here, and a merged pull
request is what releases them - the same property DATA_RELEASES.md gives
every other build input. #463 would open that pull request automatically
one day; it is deliberately post-MVP and it proposes, never publishes.
TEN PAGES, NOT NINE UPDATES. ATC's listing paginates at nine, newest first,
and it is a full archive: 89 updates on 2026-08-24, the oldest 4,252 days
(11.6 years). The 2026-08-09 spike and the 2026-08-12 review each recorded
'nine updates live' and each had read page one and stopped. #945 - The ATC
Trail Updates review only ever saw page one, and ATC's list runs to ten -
is that finding; this review is its fix, and all ten pages have now been
read.
THE TRAP IS THE SORT ORDER, so know it before reading the list again. ATC
sorts by `datePublished`, DESCENDING - verified 2026-08-24: the 89 are in
strict published order and NOT in modified order. So a notice ATC edits
every season does not move up. The three yearly bear warnings sat on page
NINE, 1,189 to 1,496 days down by the listing's own clock, having each been
edited 116 days ago. Page depth says when ATC first posted a thing and
nothing whatever about whether it is still true.
So read by `dateModified`, which every update carries in JSON-LD on its own
page, and never by listing position:
curl -s https://appalachiantrail.org/trail-updates/<slug>/ \
| grep -o '"dateModified":"[^"]*"'
WHAT A ROW CARRIES, and what it must not. Facts and a link: the mile
range, ATC's category, the states, their headline, their own last-updated
date, and the URL of their page. NOT their body text - that is ATC's
writing, and sources.json's `licence` field on `atc_trail_updates`
records why this file stops at the facts.
"atc_id": "harpers-ferry-footbridge-closure",
"title": "Harpers Ferry: Footbridge Closure",
"category": "Detour",
"states": ["MD", "WV"],
"start_mile_marker": 1026.7,
"end_mile_marker": 1026.7,
"obstructs_trail": true,
"source_url": "https://appalachiantrail.org/trail-updates/harpers-ferry-footbridge-closure/"
A POINT rather than a range - a shelter, a footbridge - is the same mile
in both markers. lib/closureSpan.ts reads that as a zero-length span and
draws it, which is right: ATC publishes several.
`obstructs_trail` IS THE ONE FIELD THAT IS NOT A FACT ABOUT ATC'S PAGE.
It is your answer to one question: is a hiker stopped from walking
through here? Only rows where that is true get drawn as a band across the
trail; the rest still reach a hiker as a banner naming the ATC.
It cannot be read off `category`, and the live page is why. Measured
Connecticut: Limestone Spring Shelter Closed   Closure   obstructs: NO
Harpers Ferry: Footbridge Closure              Detour    obstructs: YES
The only notice ATC files as `Closure` is a closed SHELTER, with the trail
past it open - and the one thing that genuinely stops a hiker, the way
across the Potomac, is filed as `Detour`. A rule reading the category is
wrong in both directions at once. When in doubt, false: losing the band
keeps the banner, and a warning that is only a banner is a smaller failure
than a barrier that is not there.
THE REVIEW BOUNDARY, which is the question #945 left open and this is the
answer. It is NOT an age cutoff. Age is the obvious rule and it is wrong
here in both directions: the standing notices are deliberately old, and a
fresh incident report can already be over.
**A row goes in when ATC's latest edit describes a CONDITION that is still
true. It stays out when that edit describes an INCIDENT that happened.**
A condition persists until something changes it, and ATC writes it that
way: a bridge swept away, a shelter closed, a spigot off, a burn ban with
an end date, a camping restriction, a legal requirement. 'remains',
'continues', 'no timeline for reopening', 'until further notice', a date
in the future.
An incident is a report of something that already happened, in the past
tense, with no ongoing-status language and no later edit: a bear that
stole a food bag at a campsite on a date, a car broken into, a person
reported missing.
The distinction is ATC's own, not one imposed on their prose, and their
posting pattern separates the two so cleanly that the boundary needed no
judgement call at the margin. Measured on the 89 live 2026-08-24: every
animal notice this review EXCLUDED as a past-season incident was last
edited 384+ days ago; every one it KEPT was edited within 154 days. A
230-day gap, with nothing in it. If a future review finds updates landing
in that gap, this rule is the thing to re-argue.
Three further rules, each of which excluded something real:
- An all-clear stays out even while ATC keeps it posted. 'NC/TN: Iron Mtn
Gap Reopened' is the standing example; this review added the Byron
Herbert Reece relocation, complete with no hazard left behind. The
counter-example is Andy Layne, ALSO a completed relocation, kept because
its edit announces a live road-walk on a road with 'little to no
shoulder'. Completed is not the test; whether a hazard survives it is.
- A stated date that has passed stays out. Harriman SP's hunting season
ends in its own text on 2025-12-31, and ATC has not said it recurs.
- A vehicle at a trailhead is not the trail. Break-ins and catalytic-
converter thefts are real and are somebody's problem to publish; they
are not a condition of the footpath this map draws.
AN UPDATE WITH NO PLACE DOES NOT GO IN THIS FILE. Two of the nine live on
2026-08-09 were like that and neither is a defect to fix: a region-wide
severe-weather advisory spanning ten states, and a law-enforcement
request that is not a place at all. Pinning either to a mile would be
actively wrong. They are real information with no home on a map yet, and
features/ATC_TRAIL_UPDATES.md leaves that an open question rather than
inventing a screen for it.
`reviewed_at` IS NOT OPTIONAL AND IS NOT THE BAKE'S DATE. It is the day a
person last checked this file against ATC's page. An empty file with no
`reviewed_at` says *nobody has looked*; an empty file WITH one says *we
looked and ATC has nothing placeable*. Only the second is publishable,
and export_atc_updates.py refuses to write an artifact without it rather
than shipping the first one dressed as the second.
`source_marker` is the ETag ATC's trail-updates feed carried at that
review. check_freshness.py compares it against the live feed, so a
STALE verdict on `atc_trail_updates` means *a person should re-read
ATC's page* - the one source in that check no automated run can clear.
Get it with:
curl -sI https://appalachiantrail.org/trail-updates/feed/ | grep -i etag
WHAT IS IN HERE NOW, reviewed 2026-08-24 against all ten pages. 89 updates
were live; 35 are here. Every row was read on its own page, and every
`updated_at` is that page's JSON-LD `dateModified`.
The other 54 break down like this, and none of them is an omission:
15  a past-season animal incident      the 384-day rule above
20  no place on the A.T.               no mile, region-wide, or off the
NOBO measure entirely
4  a vehicle at a trailhead           not a condition of the footpath
3  an all-clear                       the thing it warned about ended
2  a stated date that has passed
4  a law-enforcement request          missing persons; not the trail
1  a duplicate                        Straight Branch's A.T. closure IS
the Creeper closure, already here
5  currency unknown, so left out      see 'omit rather than guess'
FOUR ROWS OBSTRUCT THE TRAIL, up from one. Three are new and all three are
infrastructure that is simply gone, each with an official detour ATC
publishes:
Harpers Ferry: Footbridge Closure       1026.7   the way across the Potomac
SW Virginia: VA Creeper Closure        476.6-485.8  A.T. closed; reopens
2027-03-31 per the USFS
Tennessee: Nolichucky River Detour       344.6   Chestoa Bridge swept away
by Helene; no ferry in
2026, a 3.6-mile road walk
Great Gulf: Bridge Closure              1873.8   closed by the USFS, and
'hikers may be cited for
using the bridge'
The Creeper closure is worth naming twice: it is the one
features/ATC_TRAIL_UPDATES.md quotes throughout as the case this feature
exists for, it has been live and unpublished this whole time, and the
2026-08-12 review recorded it as 'gone from ATC's page' when it had only
moved to page two.
Everything else is a dot and a banner rather than a barrier. Among them,
the ones a hiker is most likely to want and could not get before: 501
Shelter and Roan High Knob and Laurel Fork and James Fry all closed with no
reopening date, Pochuck Mountain Shelter's spigot off 'for the foreseeable
future' in a section ATC says has no good natural water, Max Patch camping
shut through June 2029, Roan Mountain's burn ban to 2030, and the Pemi
Wilderness bear-canister requirement, which is a legal one.
WHAT THIS REVIEW STILL CANNOT CARRY, and it is worth writing down because
each is a real thing a hiker would want. All are excluded for the same
reason - ATC published no mile - and inventing one would be exactly the
confident wrong answer this file exists to prevent:
APPA Water System Closures (x2)   six wells closed across NY and CT
Green Mountain NF: Food Storage   a forest order over the whole VT A.T.
New York: Bear Mtn Detour         a live reroute running to summer 2027
features/ATC_TRAIL_UPDATES.md's open question about where an unplaceable
notice goes is now four notices wide rather than two, and three of them are
water or a legal requirement.
